one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with an ALL-CAPS declaration: 'CRITICS CHALLENGE the citizenship qualifications of Sen. Grace Poe to run for, be elected to and hold a higher public office allegedly because (1) as a foundling, she was stateless, (2) by her marriage, she acquired the American citizenship of her husband, and (3) her adoption by Fernando Poe Jr. and Susan Roces did not confer natural-born citizenship on her. I respectfully disagree.' Under the 1987 Constitution, natural-born citizens are 'those who are citizens of the Philippines from birth without having to perform any act to acquire or perfect their Philippine citizenship.' Since natural-born citizenship requires citizenship 'from birth' and Poe was born in 1968, the governing law is the 1935 Constitution -- which neither expressly conferred citizenship on foundlings, nor did any statute of that era. But the framers explained that an express provision was unnecessary since it could be determined from international law. Both Constitutions adopt 'the generally accepted principles of international law as part of the law of the Nation.' Under Mijares v. Ranada (April 12, 2005), such principles have two elements: (1) established, widespread and consistent state practice; and (2) opinio juris sive necessitates (a belief that the practice is obligatory). Under Article 2 of the 1961 Convention on Statelessness: 'A foundling found in the territory of a Contracting State shall, in the absence of proof to the contrary, be considered to have been born within the territory of parents possessing the nationality of that State.' Applied to Poe -- a foundling found near a church in Jaro, Iloilo, when she was only a few days old -- her parents are presumed to be Filipinos. True, the Philippines is not a signatory. However, the treaty possesses both generally-accepted-principles elements because the grant of nationality to foundlings has been an established, widespread, and consistent practice of many states since 1961. According to Razon v. Taglis (Dec 3, 2009), this international custom could be shown from State practice, legislation, international and national judicial decisions, treaties, patterns of treaties, practice of international organs, and UN General Assembly resolutions. Further, under the 1948 UDHR -- to which the Philippines is a signatory and which the SC has consistently enforced -- 'Everyone has a right to a nationality'; a denial of nationality to Poe would be a plain violation of the UDHR. CJP adds that it is 'high time the Philippines acceded to and joined the 1961 Convention on Statelessness for the benefit of all Filipinos, especially illegitimate children whose parents are unknown, not just of Senator Poe. After all, it is not their fault that their parents have abandoned them.' On American citizenship: Poe acquired it after marrying her American husband but renounced it in accordance with American law; the American Embassy affirmed this renunciation -- and under the 1930 Hague Convention, it is American, not Philippine, law that determines who are American citizens. On adoption: the SC has ruled several times that adoption does not confer citizenship -- but those rulings do not apply to foundlings; they were issued to prevent aliens from short-circuiting strict naturalization rules via adult adoption processes. Poe does not derive natural-born citizenship from adoption but from generally-accepted-principles of international law. Her presumed citizenship can become indisputable if her paternity is established by DNA evidence -- the SC has recognized DNA tests as conclusive proof of filiations since Tijing v. Court of Appeals (March 8, 2001) and People v. Vallejo (May 2, 2002). CJP will take up Poe's residence qualification in another column.
